title: Unifying enterprise apps through a shared design system
cardTitle: Design foundation for an enterprise ecosystem
summary: Tomsoft’s ERP served 200+ enterprise customers. I worked with a team building a new web-app ecosystem for existing ERP modules and new functionality. I established a shared design system on Mantine, bringing consistent patterns, branding, and a common design reference to the team.

blocks.title: From intern to leading design across apps
blocks.body:
Tomsoft’s legacy desktop ERP, Luceed, sat alongside web apps with different interfaces and interaction patterns. A planned move to React and the new Paperclip DMS created an opportunity to bring the ecosystem together around shared patterns, components, and branding, using Mantine as a foundation.

I joined as an intern and grew into owning design decisions across apps, aligning product needs with the broader design direction. I also helped hire and onboard a second designer, who focused more on the design system’s component details.

blocks.title: A shared reference for delivery
blocks.body:
There was no established design step: management’s requests went straight to developers, who had to interpret how features should work and look.

I introduced Figma as the shared reference for every feature and fix before development. Each Jira ticket linked to one Figma section, with a link back to the ticket.

Through in-person walkthroughs, I helped managers, developers, and QA use the designs, Dev Mode, variables, and component variants. Management could review the intended experience, developers had defined screens and states to build, and QA could check the result against the design, beyond whether the functionality existed.

blocks.label: Jira and Figma link to each other

items.alt: Jira ticket with an embedded Figma reference showing the document list designs and states.
Matching Figma section with document list layouts, filters, empty states, and implementation notes.

blocks.title: Common patterns across different products
blocks.body: The products served different tasks, but repeatedly needed navigation, login, invitations, permissions, and editing. Defining these patterns once gave teams a starting point for each app and users a more familiar way to work.

blocks.title: Discoverable actions and direct access
blocks.body: In an early test, four participants changed a document status’s color using two table-editing patterns: a three-dot action menu, or a clickable row opening an editor with all actions inside.

blocks.alt: Two table-editing prototypes: a three-dot menu with a focused editor, and a clickable row opening an editor with additional actions.

blocks.title: One editing pattern across tables and apps
blocks.body: Three participants preferred the menu’s clear actions; one valued row-click editing once discovered. We combined both: the three-dot menu kept all actions, with Edit first, while clicking the row opened the same editor. Duplicate, Delete, and Deactivate remained menu-only, keeping the editor focused. This became a consistent pattern across tables and apps, pairing discoverable actions with direct access.

blocks.title: A familiar way to save
blocks.body: Explicit saving matched Luceed and customers’ existing software habits, supporting continuity during adoption.

blocks.title: Extensive admin controls, a simple experience for most users
blocks.body: Admins had a second navigation with all the setup options: departments, categories, statuses, workflows, and permissions. Most users never saw this side of the app. We kept the employee interface as simple as possible, showing only the data and functionality their admin made available.

items.title: Employee
items.body: Use only what admins make available

blocks.alt: Paperclip admin interface with a separate setup navigation and a permissions matrix controlling which pages each user role can view or edit.

blocks.title: Nested setup across tabs
blocks.body: New opens a form with dropdowns for related data. Users can select an existing option or, if none is suitable, choose Add new to create that item in a new tab. The original form stays open while they set up the missing workflow, status, or city.

items.label: Our workaround
items.title: Preserved component variants
items.body: We kept important earlier versions as additional variants and used Jira and Figma notes to clarify implementation scope.

items.label: Tradeoff
items.title: Growing maintenance cost
items.body: Extra variants made the file harder to navigate and needed later cleanup. This reduced immediate confusion but did not resolve versioning.
